# P1: procedural PBR on the repo's existing stack

**Route:** three.js r186 `WebGLRenderer`, no asset files. Every mesh, texture, light probe and particle is generated by code at load. The whole prototype is one 755 KB JS file (223 KB gzipped), three.js included.

**Honest rating: 6.5/10 overall.** Close and mid shots (03, 05, 06, 07) get to about 7-7.5 and can pass for a pre-rendered game cinematic, sometimes for a CG commercial. Wide shots (01, 04) are about 5: they read as a good modern video game. Nothing here reads as TV footage of a real robot for long. See "Weak points".

## Technique in plain language

- **Geometry (`src/geo.ts`, `src/bots.ts`).** No boxes. Parts are built the way a real team builds them: laser-cut plate outlines with rounded corners, a real chamfer, and normals that stay flat on the faces and curve only across the chamfer (the mid-poly "weighted normals" trick), so a 3 mm edge catches a real highlight. Holes are real. Also modelled: socket button-head bolts, instanced roller chain with moving links, sprockets, a toothed drive belt, chevron tread blocks, weld beads as swept half-ellipses, hoses, finned motor, heat sink, pneumatic cylinder that tracks the hammer arm, ANVIL's belly, and battery packs behind the armour panel. The panel is a real separate part with a bent copy for after it tears.
- **Wear is baked per vertex.** Each vertex stores how close it is to an edge, a cavity flag and a per-part random. That replaces a Substance-style curvature bake, costs no texture memory, and survives bending. Each plate gets random UV offset and rotation, so no two plates show the same pattern.
- **Maps (`src/maps.ts`).** Generated on the GPU at load into render targets: periodic noise, Voronoi and vector scratch strokes become height, then tangent-space normals. Packed into three tiling textures: `tSteel` (normal, roughness, cavity), `tFine` (powder-coat orange peel, speckle, dust), `tMask` (chips, scratches, grime, streaks). Plus a rubber map, a smoke atlas, and a unique 2K floor painted in canvas (burns, tyre rubber, gouges, hammer scars). Albedo, metalness and AO are derived per pixel from these layers rather than stored.
- **Material (`src/uber.ts`).** One layered patch of `MeshStandardMaterial`: substrate, then paint, chips driven by edge distance, scratches, rust, grime, oil, dust, burn, then gouges. Six damage stamps per bot burn paint off exactly where hits land. Four texture samples per pixel, so it does not need triplanar.
- **Lighting (`src/arena.ts`, `src/main.ts`).** The IBL is an emissive model of the same fixture layout as the rig, filtered through PMREM. On top: a key `SunLight` with two shadow cascades, a shadowed cross spot (TV rigs give double shadows), a fill, and a flash light on each hit. A metal floor has no diffuse term, so shadow maps barely show on it: I found this in round 3. The floor is therefore partly dielectric, and each bot gets an analytic soft-box occluder that darkens reflections as well.
- **Post (`src/post.ts`).** Half-res GTAO, MSAA 4x, own dual-filter HDR bloom, AgX tone map with a punchy grade, slight chromatic aberration, vignette, grain, SMAA. The grade pass owns tone mapping and sRGB.
- **Fight (`src/fight.ts`, `src/fx.ts`).** A pure function of time: keyframed bots, hit table, closed-form particle paths (gravity, drag, floor bounce) in the vertex shader. Any frame can be seeked exactly, which is what makes `?shot=` reproducible. Sparks are stretched along velocity to imitate shutter streaks. The drum swaps to a smeared shell with translucent tooth bands above about 10 rev/s. FIRE jumps to just before TORQUE's next attack.

URL options: `?shot=<seconds>`, `?q=high|ipad|low` (touch devices default to `ipad`), `?exp=<exposure>`.

## Research

Searches were brief. Items marked [S] come from search results, not a full read of the page.

- Materials and how bots are built [S]: https://www.onlinemetals.com/en/battlebots-choosing-right-material, https://www.onlinemetals.com/en/educational-and-combat-robotics, https://robowars.org/forum/viewtopic.php?p=100419, https://news.sparkfun.com/2763, https://instructables.com/Combat-Robots, https://irobotics.illinois.edu/?p=4105
  Used for: AR500/Hardox on anything that gets hit, titanium axles, UHMW rub strips and skids, bolted replaceable teeth, chain drive, front-heavy drums, welded chassis. No source I found covered weld appearance on these bots, so bead look is from general welding knowledge.
- Edge wear from curvature, with noise breakup [S]: https://www.strayspark.studio/blog/procedural-weathering-blender-geometry-nodes, https://www.strayspark.studio/learn/tutorials/procedural-edge-wear-blender, https://polycount.com/discussion/comment/2668924
- three.js [read locally in `node_modules/three` r186.1]: `GTAOPass.js`, `SunLightShadow.js`, `shadowmap_pars_fragment.glsl.js`, `CSM.js`. CSM was rejected because it takes over `onBeforeCompile`, which the material needs. Post docs: https://threejs.org/manual/en/how-to-use-post-processing.html
- Prior repo research `.scratch/airplane-clock/research/rendering-*.md` was skimmed for the r186 facts (`SunLight` added, `PCFSoftShadowMap` removed).

## Assets and licences

None. No image, model, HDRI, font or audio file ships. Decal text uses system fonts drawn to a canvas at load. Robot names, numbers and warning plates are fictional. three.js is MIT.

## Measured

Apple M3 MacBook Air, headed Chromium with ANGLE on Metal, vsync off, over about 700 frames. **The machine was shared with five other prototypes (load average about 150), so these are noisy and likely low.** An earlier `high` run at load about 70 gave 25 fps, so the spread is wide.

| Preset | Render size | Avg fps | Median ms | p95 ms | Draws | Triangles, all passes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| high (GTAO, SMAA, MSAA 4x, 2048 shadow) | 1600x900 | 49.8 | 18.5 | 38.0 | about 420 | 1.5M |
| ipad (GTAO, MSAA 4x, 1536 shadow, no SMAA) | 1419x986 | 60.3 | 15.0 | 34.2 | about 390 | 1.5M |
| low (no GTAO, MSAA 2x, 1024 shadow) | 1073x746 | 156 | 5.0 | 17.0 | about 240 | 1.0M |

- Unique triangles were about 500K at the last profile, before later small additions. Bolts, chain and welds are left out of shadow and AO passes, which took a frame from 3.9M to 1.5M.
- Download: 755 KB JS, 223 KB gzip. `dist/` is 744 KB. No other files, no network requests after the page and JS (verified from a sub-path on a plain static server).
- Load: about 1.5 s to first frame on the Mac. GPU map generation 100-400 ms, up to 1.8 s under the worst load.
- `shots/clip.webm` is 36 MB because it is a high-quality review capture, rendered frame by frame at 30 fps, so it is not a live capture and says nothing about real-time speed. It is not part of the download.

## iPad (estimate, not tested)

Based on the M3 numbers, not on an iPad.

- **M-series iPad:** likely holds 30 fps on `ipad` at about 1.4 MP. It may reach 60 until it warms up.
- **Base A-series iPad:** its GPU is far weaker than an M3 (my estimate is about a third). Expect about 20-30 fps on `ipad`, so ship `low`, or `ipad` without GTAO at about 1 MP.
- **Risks I could not measure:** 400 draw calls through Safari's WebGL layer, shader compile stalls on first use, about 35 program variants, thermal throttling in sustained play, and half-float MSAA memory. Tile-based GPUs should make MSAA cheap. GTAO and shadows are the real cost. There is no automatic quality governor yet.

## To reach production

1. Move to `src/<game>/arena/three/` behind the same stage interface the other games use. Geometry and maps generate at load, so nothing changes in the PWA cache. Tree-shaking should trim the JS.
2. Pre-compile shaders behind the loading screen with `compileAsync`. Add a governor that steps quality down on sustained frame drops, and pause rendering when hidden.
3. Merge draws: bots to one material with a small palette texture, and static arena into fewer batches. Target under 150 draws.
4. Cache generated maps, or run the generator at build time, if slow iPads take too long.
5. Replace the keyframed fight with a small scripted variation system so it does not repeat exactly, and tie FIRE to it. Add sound. Replace `__dump`/`__tex` debug hooks.
6. Test on the real iPad first. That result should decide presets.

Estimated effort: 1-2 weeks after a real iPad test, more if each bot needs customisation. Modelling new bots in code is slow, about a day each. That is the true cost of this route.

## Weak points

- **Wide shots look like a game.** Light on the floor is too even, and there is no global illumination or true floor reflection, so bots do not sit in the room as they do up close.
- **Only one environment probe**, so reflections do not change as a bot moves. Bots do not reflect each other or the arena properly.
- **The arena surroundings are close to a void.** The polycarbonate walls are barely visible and do not read as thick, scratched panels. I could not get past "opaque" or "invisible" in the time given. The truss is almost never in frame.
- **Damage is painted on.** Plates do not dent. The panel swaps to a pre-bent copy with faceted normals, and the swap is hidden only by the sparks.
- **No general motion blur or depth of field.** Long-lens TV footage relies on both. Only sparks and the drum fake it.
- **Procedural surfaces repeat in character.** Wear looks plausible but evenly distributed, with no story. A scanned or hand-painted asset beats it up close. Floor gouges get thin and dashed at distance, and burn marks can read as shallow dents.
- **Smoke is unlit billboards**, with no soft depth fade. Fine in motion, flat in a still.
- **The bots still look slightly designed** rather than built. Hammer proportions are theatrical, and motion is keyframed with no physics, so hits land with less weight in motion than the stills suggest.
- **Machine-load caveat:** the fps table is one noisy run.

**Limit of the route:** zero asset weight gets surprisingly far on edges, wear and mid-range detail. What stops it is lighting and capture, not modelling. Getting to "TV footage" needs GI or path-traced light, and that does not fit this renderer on an iPad.
